title: AI for Productivity
description: Applying what you have learned to the work you actually do every week.

lessons.title: AI for students
lessons.description: Understand better, never avoid understanding -- and the loop that proves the difference.
lessons.content:
## Learn

This is the module where the course starts paying for itself. Everything from here is applied.

A principle first, because it decides whether AI helps you or hurts you as a student.

### The line that matters

**Use AI to understand better. Do not use it to avoid understanding.**

Those produce identical-looking output in the short term and completely different results in an exam, an interview, or a job.

Asking for an explanation of something you did not follow in a lecture is learning. Asking for an essay you submit as your own is not, and it also leaves you unable to discuss what you submitted.

The honest test: **would you be comfortable if your tutor watched how you used it?** If not, that is worth paying attention to rather than arguing with.

Check your institution's actual policy. They vary widely and they are enforced.

### What genuinely helps

**Explaining at your level.** *"Explain Bayes' theorem to someone who understands basic probability but has never seen this. One worked example with small numbers."* Better than a textbook precisely because you can specify where you are.

**The same idea three ways.** When one explanation does not land, ask for another with a different analogy. This is something a textbook cannot do and a busy lecturer often cannot either.

**Practice questions.** Give it your material and ask for questions, then answer them before looking. Testing yourself is one of the few study techniques with strong evidence behind it, and generating questions used to be the hard part.

**Checking your understanding.** Explain a concept in your own words, paste it, and ask what you got wrong or left out. This is the single most valuable study use of AI, and almost nobody does it.

**Finding the gap.** *"I understand X but not Y. What is the concept between them that I am missing?"* Often exactly the right question.

**Structure and feedback on your own work.** Outlines, and critique of a draft you wrote.

### What to be careful with

**Facts, dates, citations and formulas.** Module 3 applies in full. Verify anything you will be marked on.

**Anything you submit.** Know your institution's rules and follow them.

**Explanations in unfamiliar territory.** A confident wrong explanation is worse than no explanation, and you cannot catch it in a subject you are new to. Cross-check against your actual course materials.

**The feeling of understanding.** Reading a good explanation feels like learning and is not. The test is whether you can reproduce it without looking. Close the tab and write it out.

## Demonstrate

The highest-value study loop, in four steps. Try it on something you are learning this week.

1. **Write your own explanation** of the concept, from memory, in your own words. Badly is fine.
2. **Paste it** with: *"This is my understanding of X. What have I got wrong, what have I oversimplified, and what have I left out? Do not rewrite it -- tell me what to fix."*
3. **Fix it yourself** based on what it said.
4. **Paste the fixed version** and ask again.

Step 1 is the one people skip, and it is where all the learning is. Writing from memory before you look anything up is retrieval practice, and it is far more effective than rereading.

The AI's role here is a patient reviewer who never gets bored. That is a genuinely new thing for a student to have.

## Practice

Pick a concept from your current studies that you think you understand.

Do the four-step loop above. Record what the review caught.

Most people find at least one thing they had confidently wrong. That is the point, and it is much better to find it now than in an exam.

Then, separately: generate ten practice questions from a topic, answer them without looking, and mark yourself. Note your score.

## What to remember

- Use AI to understand better, never to avoid understanding
- Explain it yourself first, then ask what you got wrong
- Generating practice questions is cheap and testing yourself works
- Reading a good explanation feels like learning; reproducing it is learning
- Know your institution's policy, and verify anything you will be marked on

lessons.title: AI for research
lessons.description: Shape, vocabulary and critique from AI; facts and citations from real sources.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Research is where AI is most useful and most dangerous, often in the same session.

### The split that keeps you safe

**Safe: using AI to navigate and understand.**

- What are the main positions in this debate?
- What should I read first on this topic?
- Explain this paper's method in plain language
- What is this field's jargon, and what do the terms mean?
- Summarise this paper I have uploaded
- What questions should I be asking about this?

**Dangerous: using AI as the source.**

- Give me five papers on this
- What is the statistic for X?
- What did author Y conclude?
- Quote the relevant passage

The first list asks for **shape and explanation**. The second asks for **facts it would have to recall** -- which is exactly where module 3 said invention clusters.

Structure your research around the first list, and get facts from actual sources.

### Where AI genuinely accelerates research

**Orientation in an unfamiliar field.** Two hours of reading compressed into ten minutes of asking, giving you the vocabulary and the shape of the debate so that real reading is productive.

**Understanding difficult papers.** Upload it and ask about the method, the assumptions, what the limitations section really means. Grounded in the paper in front of it, this is reliable.

**Finding the question.** Describe what you are curious about and ask what the field calls it. Often the hardest part of research is knowing the term to search for.

**Summarising material you have.** Transformation, not recall. Safe.

**Critiquing your own argument.** *"What would a sceptical reviewer say about this?"* Genuinely useful and uncomfortable in the right way.

### The citation problem, restated

Do not ask a general assistant for references. It will produce plausible ones, some real and some not, indistinguishable from each other.

Use a search-first tool that shows sources, or a real academic database, and then use AI to help you **understand** what you found.

This division -- databases for finding, AI for understanding -- is the whole method.

### A workflow that works

1. Ask AI for the **shape** of the topic and the **vocabulary**
2. Use a real database or search tool to find actual sources
3. Upload the sources you found and use AI to understand them
4. Write your own argument
5. Ask AI to critique it
6. Verify every fact and citation yourself

AI appears in four of six steps and never as the source of a fact.

## Demonstrate

Take a topic you know nothing about. Genuinely nothing -- that is the point.

**Step one, orientation.**

> I know nothing about [topic]. Give me the shape of the field: the main questions people are trying to answer, the main positions, and the vocabulary I need to read about it. Do not cite specific papers, authors or statistics -- I will find those myself. Where the field is genuinely unsettled, say so.

Note that the prompt removes the hallucination risk by not asking for the risky thing. That is lesson 11 of module 4 in practice.

**Step two.** Take the vocabulary you just learned and search a real database with it. Notice how much better your searches are now.

**Step three.** Upload something you found and ask what its method actually is and what its limitations section really admits.

The whole sequence takes twenty minutes and replaces an afternoon of poorly-targeted reading.

## Practice

Do the three steps above on a topic you genuinely need to understand.

Then deliberately do the dangerous thing: ask a general assistant for five references on that topic. Look up every one.

Record how many were real, how many were plausible fabrications, and -- importantly -- whether you could tell the difference before checking.

That last answer is usually no, and it is the most useful thing this lesson can teach you.

## What to remember

- Use AI for shape, vocabulary, explanation and critique
- Never use it as the source of a fact, a statistic or a citation
- Databases and search tools for finding; AI for understanding what you found
- Uploading a paper and asking about it is safe; asking about it from memory is not
- Asking what a sceptical reviewer would say is uncomfortable and valuable

lessons.title: AI for presentations
lessons.description: Decide the argument before you make a single slide.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Most presentations fail before a slide is made, because the argument was never decided. AI helps most at that stage, and least at the stage people use it for.

### Where it actually helps

**Finding the argument.** Before any slides: *"I need to persuade X of Y in ten minutes. What is the strongest structure, and what will they object to?"* This is the highest-value use and almost nobody does it.

**The outline.** Slide-by-slide, with one sentence per slide saying what that slide is for. A deck where each slide has a stated job is better than one assembled from whatever came to mind.

**Cutting.** Paste your outline and ask what to remove to fit the time. Ruthless editing is easier when something else suggests the cuts.

**Speaker notes.** From your slides, which is transformation and therefore reliable.

**Anticipating questions.** *"What are the five hardest questions I will be asked, and what is a good answer to each?"* This is the single best preparation you can do, and it is tedious to do alone.

**Rehearsal feedback.** Paste what you plan to say and ask where it is unclear, too long, or assumes something the audience will not know.

### Where it helps less than promised

**Generating whole decks.** Several tools will produce a complete presentation from a prompt. What you get is generic, evenly-weighted, and has no argument. It looks like a presentation and does not do what a presentation is for.

If you use one, treat it as a first draft of the **structure** and rewrite the content.

**Design.** Tools that auto-design slides produce something tidy and anonymous. Fine for internal use, weak where it matters.

### The rule for slides

A slide is not a document. AI defaults to complete sentences and full paragraphs, which is exactly wrong for a slide.

Ask explicitly: *"Six words maximum per line, at most four lines per slide, no full sentences."* And put the full prose in the speaker notes, which is where it belongs.

### The time budget

If you have two hours for a presentation, spending twenty minutes with AI on the argument and the likely objections is a better investment than two hours on slides. Almost everyone does the reverse.

## Demonstrate

The argument-first workflow. Try it on a presentation you actually have to give.

**One: the argument.**

> I have ten minutes to persuade [audience] that [claim]. They currently believe [what they think now] and they care most about [their priority]. What is the strongest structure for this argument, and what are the three objections I should expect?

**Two: the outline.** Take the structure and ask for a slide-by-slide outline, with one sentence per slide stating what that slide is for.

**Three: the cut.** *"This is more than ten minutes. What comes out first, and why?"*

**Four: the questions.** *"What are the five hardest questions this audience will ask, and what is a good answer to each?"*

Now build the slides yourself. You have an argument, a structure, a defensible length and prepared answers. That is the hard part done, and no deck-generating tool would have produced any of it.

## Practice

Take a presentation you have to give, or one you gave recently and could have given better.

Run the four steps. Compare the resulting structure with what you would have done.

Then do the objections exercise properly: write your answers to the five hardest questions before looking at the suggested ones. Compare.

Most people find at least one question they had not considered, and that alone justifies the twenty minutes.

## What to remember

- Decide the argument before making any slides; this is where AI helps most
- Ask what objections to expect and prepare answers
- Auto-generated decks look like presentations without being one
- Tell it explicitly that slides are not prose, or you will get paragraphs
- Twenty minutes on the argument beats two hours on slides

lessons.title: AI for spreadsheets
lessons.content:
## Learn

Spreadsheets are where AI removes a specific, widespread frustration: knowing exactly what you want and not knowing the formula.

### The three things it does well

**Writing formulas from a description.** *"I need a formula that sums column D only where column B is 'completed' and column A is in the last 30 days."* You get the formula, and usually an explanation.

**Explaining a formula someone else wrote.** Paste a nested monster you inherited and ask what it does. Genuinely one of the best uses, and it makes inherited spreadsheets far less frightening.

**Debugging.** *"This returns an error. Here is the formula and what the columns contain. What is wrong?"*

### The two things it does badly

**Arithmetic.** Do not ask it to compute values. Ask it for the **formula** and let the spreadsheet compute. Module 3 explained why: it produces plausible-looking numbers, not calculated ones.

This distinction is the whole safety rule for this lesson. **Formulas yes, figures no.**

**Reading numbers off a screenshot.** Also module 3. It will misread a digit confidently.

### Getting good formulas first time

Three things to include:

**The exact column letters and what is in them.** "Column C contains dates as real dates, not text" prevents a whole class of wrong answer.

**Which spreadsheet program.** Excel and Google Sheets differ in function names and behaviour. Say which.

**What to do about the awkward cases.** Blanks, errors, text where numbers should be. If you do not say, you get a formula that breaks on the first blank row.

A good request looks like:

> Google Sheets. Column A has dates (real dates), column B has status text which is 'completed', 'pending' or 'cancelled', column D has amounts as numbers with some blanks.
>
> I need the total of column D where status is 'completed' and the date is within the last 30 days from today. Blanks in D should count as zero, not break the formula.
>
> Give me the formula and one sentence on how it works.

### Pivot tables and analysis

Describing what you want a pivot table to show and asking how to build it works well. So does asking which chart type suits a particular comparison, and why.

For analysing actual data, the safer route is uploading the file to a tool that runs code -- then the numbers are computed rather than predicted. Check that it read your columns correctly before trusting anything after.

## Demonstrate

Two exercises, ten minutes, both worth doing.

**One: the inherited formula.** Find the most complicated formula in any spreadsheet you have -- yours or someone else's. Paste it and ask what it does, step by step.

Then check the explanation against what the cell actually shows. Most people find the explanation correct and immediately more useful than the formula.

**Two: formulas versus figures.** Take a column of about twenty numbers.

Ask the tool to add them up in its answer. Then compute the same sum in the spreadsheet.

Compare. Sometimes it is right. The point is that you cannot tell which times without checking, which is why the rule is formulas, not figures.

## Practice

Take a real spreadsheet task you have been avoiding because you did not know how.

Write the request with all three ingredients: column letters and contents, which program, and what to do about awkward cases.

Get the formula, use it, and check the result against a case you can verify by hand.

Then write down what you would have done before -- searched, asked someone, done it manually -- and how long that would have taken.

## What to remember

- Formulas yes, figures no; let the spreadsheet do the arithmetic
- Explaining an inherited formula is one of the best uses available
- Say which program, give the column letters, and state what to do about blanks
- Upload the file if you want real analysis, then check it parsed your columns
- Never take a number off a screenshot without verifying it

lessons.title: AI for documents
lessons.description: You supply the substance, AI handles the shape.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Document work is the most common use of AI and the one people get least value from, because they ask for the wrong thing.

### Ask for a draft, not a document

The instinct is "write me a report". What comes back is generic, evenly weighted, and requires as much editing as writing would have.

The productive pattern is narrower:

- Write the section I am stuck on
- Rewrite this paragraph for a different audience
- Tighten this without losing anything
- Give me three ways to open this
- What is missing from this outline?

Small, specific requests on material you already have produce far better results than one large request from nothing.

### The shape that works

**You provide the substance. AI handles the shape.**

You know what the report should say. You know the constraints, the politics, the history. The tool does not, and it cannot guess. What it is good at is turning your substance into prose, restructuring it, and adjusting the register.

So: write your thinking down badly, quickly, in bullets. Then ask for it to be turned into the document. That is transformation, which is reliable, rather than generation, which is generic.

### Where it is genuinely strong

**Changing register.** The same content for a colleague, an executive, a customer, a regulator. This is hard for people and easy for AI.

**Tightening.** *"Cut this by 30 per cent without losing any substantive point. Tell me what you removed."* The last clause is important: it lets you overrule a cut.

**Structure.** Paste a messy document and ask for a better structure with a reason for the new order.

**Consistency.** Checking a long document for contradictions, inconsistent terminology or repeated points.

**The blank page.** Three possible openings, to react to. Reacting is much easier than starting.

**Filling a template.** You have a standard format; you have the raw information; the tool does the assembly.

### Editing your own writing

The most valuable and least used request:

> Here is my draft. Do not rewrite it. Tell me: which sentences are unclear, which claims are unsupported, where the structure works against the argument, and what a reader would ask that I have not answered.

Critique keeps your voice and improves your thinking. Rewriting replaces both. Most people ask for the rewrite.

### What to watch

**Your voice disappears.** Heavily AI-edited writing converges on a recognisable middle register -- fluent, slightly bland, faintly corporate. If your writing has character, protect it. Accept edits selectively.

**Confident additions.** A rewrite can add a claim you never made. Read for things you did not say, not just for phrasing.

**Disclosure.** Some contexts require you to say AI was involved. Know the rules where you are.

## Demonstrate

Turn thinking into a document. Try it with something real.

**One.** Write down what you want to say, in bullets, badly, in five minutes. No editing, no structure, just get it out.

**Two.**

> Below are my rough notes for a [document type] aimed at [audience]. Turn them into a first draft. Use only what is in the notes -- if something important is missing, list it at the end under "gaps" rather than inventing it. Around [N] words. [Tone].

**Three.** Now critique rather than rewrite:

> Do not rewrite. Tell me which sentences are unclear, which claims I have not supported, and what a sceptical reader would ask that I have not answered.

**Four.** Fix it yourself.

The gaps list in step two is the part people are surprised by. It tells you what you have not actually thought about yet, which is more valuable than the draft.

## Practice

Take a document you owe someone.

Do the four steps. Time yourself and compare with how long it would normally take.

Then look specifically at step three's output. Count how many of the criticisms you agree with. Most people find roughly half are useful, and the useful half is worth more than the draft.

## What to remember

- You supply the substance; AI handles the shape
- Small specific requests beat one large "write me a report"
- Ask for critique, not rewriting, when it is your own writing
- The "gaps" instruction tells you what you have not thought about
- Watch for your voice being sanded off, and for claims you never made

lessons.title: AI for email
lessons.description: Routine replies for speed, difficult emails for a version you did not write while annoyed.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Email is where AI saves the most time for the most people, because so much of it is formulaic.

### The three genuinely useful cases

**The routine reply.** Confirmations, acknowledgements, scheduling, standard answers. Little judgement needed, and AI handles it in seconds.

**The difficult email.** A complaint, a refusal, a delivery of bad news, a disagreement with someone senior. Here the value is not speed -- it is getting a version that is not the one you would write while annoyed.

**The long thread.** Summarising fifteen messages into what was decided and what is outstanding, before you reply.

### The difficult email is the real win

Most people underuse this. When you need to write something awkward, the useful move is not "write this email" but:

> I need to tell a client we will miss a deadline by two weeks. It is our fault -- a supplier issue we should have caught. They have been patient before. I want to be honest, not over-apologise, and propose something concrete.
>
> Give me three versions with different levels of directness. Do not invent any explanation or commitment beyond what I said.

Three versions to react to is much easier than one to accept or reject. And the final clause matters: without it you get an invented reason or a promise you cannot keep.

### The summarise-before-replying habit

For any thread over about ten messages:

> Summarise this thread: what was decided, what is still open, who owes what, and what I specifically have been asked for. Quote the message each point comes from.

The "quote the message" instruction converts it from a summary you must trust into one you can check in seconds.

### Rules worth keeping

**Read every word before sending.** Obvious, routinely ignored, and the failure is public.

**Never paste confidential material into a tool your organisation has not approved.** Email is full of things that should not leave the building, and it is the easiest place to do this without thinking.

**Do not let it invent facts.** Dates, amounts, commitments, reasons. Include "use only what I have given you" on anything with specifics.

**Match your normal voice.** A reply that reads nothing like you is noticed, particularly by people who know you.

**Some emails should not be AI-assisted.** Condolences. A personal apology. Anything where the fact that you wrote it is the point. Sending a generated message in these cases is worse than sending nothing.

### The system prompt that pays for itself

Set standing instructions once:

> When drafting emails for me: British English, no exclamation marks, no "I hope this email finds you well", get to the point in the first sentence, sign off with "Best". Keep routine replies under 80 words.

Every draft afterwards is closer to right. This is the highest-value five minutes in this module.

## Demonstrate

Take a genuinely awkward email you need to send. If you have none, use: telling a colleague their work needs redoing.

Run the difficult-email pattern: state the situation, the relationship, what you want to achieve, and ask for three versions of varying directness, with the no-invention constraint.

Read all three. You will probably take the structure of one and the opening of another. That is the intended use -- material to react to, not a message to send.

Then, separately: find your longest recent thread and run the summarise-before-replying prompt. Check two of the quotes against the actual messages.

## Practice

Set your email system prompt. Be specific: language, greeting, sign-off, length, tone, anything you never want to see.

Then draft three real emails with it and count how much editing each needed. Adjust the instructions based on what you kept fixing.

That adjustment loop is exactly module 4's iterative prompting, applied to something you do twenty times a day.

## What to remember

- Routine replies for speed, difficult emails for a version you did not write while annoyed
- Ask for three versions of a hard email, not one
- Summarise long threads before replying, with quotes so you can check
- Always add "use only what I have given you" when specifics are involved
- Some emails should never be AI-assisted, and sending one is worse than sending nothing

lessons.title: AI for meeting summaries
lessons.description: Decisions, owners and open questions -- and what a transcript always misses.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Meeting summaries are among the most reliably valuable uses of AI, because the material is entirely in front of the tool. This is transformation, not recall.

### What good looks like

A useful summary is not a narrative of the meeting. Nobody wants a retelling. It answers four questions:

1. **What was decided?**
2. **What is still open?**
3. **Who is doing what, by when?**
4. **What would someone who missed it need to know?**

Ask for those four things explicitly. Ask for "a summary" and you get a retelling.

### The prompt

> Below is a transcript of a meeting.
>
> [transcript]
>
> Produce:
> 1. One sentence on what the meeting was about
> 2. Decisions made
> 3. Open questions, with who needs to resolve each
> 4. Action items, each with an owner and a date if one was stated
>
> Rules:
> - Use only what is in the transcript
> - If an action has no clear owner, write "owner not stated" rather than guessing
> - If no decisions were made, say so rather than inventing one
> - Quote the transcript for each decision

The last four lines do the work. Without them you get invented owners, invented decisions, and a tidy summary of a meeting that decided nothing.

### Where the transcript comes from

Many meeting tools now transcribe and summarise automatically. Where yours does, use it and apply the checks below.

Where it does not, most devices will transcribe a recording, and any assistant will summarise the transcript.

**Before recording anyone, get their agreement.** This is a legal requirement in many places and a basic courtesy everywhere. Recording a meeting without telling people is not a technical decision.

### What summaries reliably miss

**Tone and reluctance.** "Fine, we will do it that way" reads in a transcript exactly like agreement. It frequently was not.

**Silence.** Nobody objecting is not the same as everybody agreeing, and a transcript cannot tell the difference.

**Who actually has the authority.** A summary attributes an action to whoever said they would do it, which is not always who can.

**Context from outside the room.** Half of most meetings makes sense only if you know what happened last month.

So: a summary is a record of the **words**. For a meeting that mattered, it is a useful artefact and not a substitute for having been there.

### The habit

Send the summary to attendees and ask for corrections before treating it as the record. This takes a minute, catches misattributed actions, and converts a generated document into an agreed one.

## Demonstrate

Take a recording or transcript of a real meeting -- with the participants' knowledge.

Run the prompt above. Then do the check properly:

1. Go through the action items. Is each owner right? Did anyone get assigned something they did not agree to?
2. Look at the decisions. Was each one actually decided, or did the conversation just move on?
3. Think about what is missing. What did you know from being there that is not in the summary?

That third question is where the lesson is. Write down the answer.

## Practice

Do the above for one real meeting.

Then send the summary to one other attendee and ask what it got wrong.

Record their corrections. Most people get at least one, and it is usually an action item attributed to the wrong person -- exactly the failure that causes trouble later.

## What to remember

- Ask for decisions, open questions, actions and owners, not "a summary"
- Include "owner not stated" and "say so if no decisions were made"
- Ask for a transcript quote per decision so you can check
- Get agreement before recording anyone
- It records words, not reluctance, silence or authority
- Send it round for correction before treating it as the record

lessons.title: AI for brainstorming
lessons.description: Ask for thirty, constrain for variety, then have it attack your favourite.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Brainstorming is one of the few uses where the model's lack of judgement is an advantage. You want volume and variety; you supply the judgement afterwards.

### Ask for more than you need

Ask for five ideas and you get five safe ones. Ask for thirty and something interesting appears around number twenty, once the obvious ones are used up.

> Give me 30 ideas for [X]. Do not filter for quality or feasibility -- I want range. Include some that are obvious, some unusual, and at least five that seem impractical.

Explicitly permitting bad ideas matters. Left to itself the model produces reasonable, sensible, forgettable suggestions.

### Constrain to get variety

Unconstrained brainstorming converges on the obvious. Constraints force it elsewhere.

- *"...if the budget were zero"*
- *"...if we had to launch next week"*
- *"...that a competitor would hate"*
- *"...that would work for someone with no internet access"*
- *"...that deliberately break our usual approach"*

Each produces a different set. Running four constrained rounds beats one unconstrained round by a wide margin.

### Use it to attack, not only to generate

The most valuable brainstorming use is adversarial:

> Here is my plan. Give me the fifteen strongest objections, ordered by how likely they are to actually kill it. For each, say what evidence would tell me whether it is a real problem.

This is uncomfortable and extremely useful. People are bad at attacking their own ideas and a tool has no ego about it.

Related, and also good: *"What would have to be true for this to work? Which of those is least certain?"*

### Building on your own ideas

Brainstorming works better from something than from nothing.

> Here are my six ideas. For each: a version that is more ambitious, a version that is cheaper, and the strongest objection.

Eighteen outputs from six inputs, all grounded in your thinking rather than the model's defaults.

### What it cannot do

**It does not know your situation.** The constraints, the politics, the history, what was tried in 2021 and failed. Supply those or the ideas are generic.

**It cannot judge.** Feasibility, cost, whether your team would tolerate it -- all yours.

**It produces the average.** Trained on what people have written, it tends toward what people have already thought of. Genuinely novel ideas usually come from you; the model is good at variations, combinations and objections.

That last point is worth being clear-eyed about. This is an excellent tool for widening a search and a poor one for original insight.

## Demonstrate

The four-round method, on something real.

**Round 1: volume.** 30 ideas, no filtering, some deliberately impractical.

**Round 2: constraints.** Take the same brief and run it four more times with four different constraints.

**Round 3: combine.** *"Here are the six most interesting from those lists. Combine them into five new ideas that take something from more than one."*

**Round 4: attack.** Pick your favourite. Ask for the fifteen strongest objections ordered by lethality, with the evidence that would settle each.

You end with a wide set, a shortlist you built, and a clear-eyed view of what could kill the winner. Twenty-five minutes.

## Practice

Take a decision or problem you are actually sitting on.

Run all four rounds. Keep every list.

Then mark the ideas: how many were obvious, how many were useless, how many were genuinely worth considering?

The ratio is usually something like twenty obvious, eight useless, two worth pursuing. Two good ideas for twenty-five minutes is a good trade, and you should calibrate your expectations to that rather than to hoping for brilliance.

## What to remember

- Ask for thirty, not five, and explicitly permit bad ideas
- Constraints produce variety; run several constrained rounds
- Adversarial use -- the fifteen strongest objections -- is the highest-value application
- Feed it your own ideas and ask for variations and attacks
- Good at widening the search, poor at original insight; supply your situation or get generic output

lessons.title: AI for learning
lessons.description: The techniques that work, each made easier, and the illusion to watch for.
lessons.content:
## Learn

This lesson is about learning anything, at any age, for any reason -- not only formal study.

### What AI changes about learning

Three things, and they are real.

**An explanation pitched at you.** Books and courses are written for an imagined average reader. You can ask for the version that starts where you actually are.

**Infinite patience.** You can ask the same question five times, admit you did not follow it, and ask for a completely different angle. Nobody is sighing.

**Practice on demand.** Questions, exercises, scenarios, generated from whatever you are learning, in unlimited supply.

### What it does not change

**Learning still requires effort from you.** Reading a good explanation is not learning. Retrieving, practising and being wrong is learning. The tool makes the input better; it cannot do the work.

This is worth being blunt about, because the input being so much better creates a strong illusion of progress.

### The techniques that work, with AI attached

Learning science is fairly settled on what works. Each of these is now easier.

**Retrieval practice** -- recalling from memory rather than rereading. Ask for questions, answer them without looking, then check.

**Spaced repetition** -- revisiting at increasing intervals. Ask for questions on what you learned last week and last month, mixed in.

**Interleaving** -- mixing topics rather than blocking them. *"Give me twenty questions mixing everything from this course so far, in random order."* Harder than it feels it should be, and that is the point.

**Elaboration** -- explaining why and how, connecting to what you know. *"How does this connect to X, which I already understand?"*

**The Feynman technique** -- explain it simply and find where you cannot. This is the loop from lesson 1 and it is the best single use of AI for learning.

**Worked examples, then fading.** Ask for a fully worked example, then one with the last step removed, then one with the last two removed. Excellent for anything procedural.

### The traps

**Fluency mistaken for understanding.** The explanations are so clear that following them feels like learning. Close the tab and write it from memory. That is the only reliable test.

**Never being stuck.** Productive struggle is where learning happens, and instant answers remove it. Impose a rule: try for ten minutes before asking. The difficulty is not a bug in your study process.

**Confident wrong explanations in a new field.** You cannot catch them, by definition. Cross-check against a real source for anything foundational.

**Breadth without depth.** It is easy to learn the shape of twenty topics and none of them properly. Decide which you actually want to be able to do.

## Demonstrate

A complete study session for anything, in six steps. Use it this week on something real.

1. **Orient.** *"I want to learn X. I already know Y. What is the sequence of concepts, in order, and what is the first one?"*
2. **Learn** the first concept from a real source, not from the model.
3. **Explain it back** from memory, in writing.
4. **Get critique.** *"This is my understanding. What is wrong, oversimplified, or missing? Do not rewrite it."*
5. **Practise.** *"Five questions on this, increasing in difficulty. Do not give me the answers yet."*
6. **Check and repeat**, adding last session's material to step 5.

Step 2 matters more than it looks. Learning the foundations from a real source and using the model for explanation, critique and practice keeps confident wrong explanations out of your foundations.

## Practice

Choose something you have wanted to learn and not started.

Run steps 1 and 2 now. Actually do step 3 -- write your explanation from memory.

Then run step 4 and record what the critique caught.

Set yourself the ten-minute rule for the next week: no asking until you have tried for ten minutes. Note at the end of the week how often you solved it yourself in minutes six to ten.

## What to remember

- An explanation pitched at you, infinite patience, and unlimited practice questions
- The techniques that work are unchanged; AI makes each of them easier
- Fluency is not understanding; close the tab and write it from memory
- Struggle for ten minutes before asking, deliberately
- Learn foundations from a real source; use AI for explanation, critique and practice

lessons.title: AI-powered search
lessons.description: You outsourced source evaluation; click one source and see how it went.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Search has changed in a way worth understanding, because the failure mode changed with it.

### The old model and the new one

Traditional search gives you **a list of places to look**. You judge the sources, you read them, you form a view. Slow, and the judgement stays with you.

AI-powered search gives you **an answer**, assembled from sources it read for you. Much faster, and the judgement has moved to the machine.

That shift is the whole thing. You have outsourced source evaluation, and you cannot see how it went unless you look.

### What this is genuinely good for

**Questions that used to take five tabs.** Comparisons, "what is the difference between", "how do I do X in Y" -- where the answer was spread across several pages.

**Getting oriented.** A quick shape of an unfamiliar topic.

**Finding the right words.** When you do not know the term for what you are looking for, describing it works where searching could not.

**Questions with a definite answer.** Conversions, definitions, how a well-documented thing works.

### Where it fails

**Contested topics.** Where sources genuinely disagree, a synthesised answer flattens the disagreement into false consensus. You cannot see that from the answer.

**Thin coverage.** A topic with little good material online produces an answer assembled from poor sources, delivered in the same confident format as a well-sourced one.

**Anything recent or fast-moving.** What was found may be out of date, and the answer will not say so.

**Commercial questions.** "Best X for Y" pulls heavily from affiliate content and marketing. The synthesis inherits the bias and hides its origin.

**When you needed the sources.** If you will be quoted on it, a summary is not enough.

### The habit

**Click at least one source. Always.**

Not to verify every claim -- to see what kind of material the answer was built from. Official documentation and a peer-reviewed paper is a different situation from a content-farm article and a forum post, and the answer looks identical either way.

This takes ten seconds and is the single most valuable habit in this lesson.

### When to use which

Use **AI search** for orientation, definite answers, and questions spread across several pages.

Use **traditional search** when the topic is contested, when you need to judge sources yourself, when currency matters, and when the question is commercial.

Use **both** when it matters: get the shape from one and verify from the other.

### The longer-term concern

Worth naming. If most people read synthesised answers rather than visiting sources, the people who write those sources get less traffic and less reason to write. The synthesis depends on material that the synthesis makes less viable to produce.

Nobody knows how that resolves. It is a reason to click through to sources that are useful to you, beyond your own verification needs.

## Demonstrate

Three searches, one habit.

**One: a definite answer.** Something with a single correct answer you can verify. Ask an AI search tool. Check it. This is where the technology is at its best.

**Two: something contested.** A question in your own field where knowledgeable people disagree. Ask the same tool.

Does the answer acknowledge the disagreement, or does it produce a tidy consensus? Click the sources. Do they actually agree with each other?

**Three: something commercial.** "Best X for Y" in a category you know. Look at the sources. Count how many are trying to sell you something or earn a commission.

Exercise three is the one that changes behaviour. Most people are surprised.

## Practice

For one week, click at least one source on every AI search result you rely on.

Keep a tally: how often were the sources what you expected, and how often were they weaker?

Most people find the rate of weak sources much higher than they assumed, and concentrated exactly in commercial and contested questions -- which are the ones where being misled costs the most.

## What to remember

- You have outsourced source evaluation; the only way to see how it went is to look
- Good for orientation, definite answers, and questions spread over several pages
- Weak on contested topics, thin coverage, recency and commercial questions
- Click at least one source, every time -- ten seconds, highest value habit here
- A tidy answer over poor sources looks identical to a good one

lessons.title: Practice questions and answer key
lessons.description: Ten questions covering the whole module, with a full explanation for each.
lessons.content:
Ten questions on the whole of module 6.

:::quiz
Q. What is the most valuable study use of AI, and the one almost nobody does?
- Asking it to summarise your lecture notes
+ Writing your own explanation from memory, then asking what you got wrong
- Asking it to generate an essay outline
- Asking it to explain a concept three different ways
= Writing from memory first is retrieval practice, which is one of the few study techniques with strong evidence behind it. The AI's role is a patient reviewer that never gets bored. Skipping step one and going straight to a good explanation feels like learning and is not.

Q. Which research request is safe, and which is dangerous?
- Both "summarise this paper I uploaded" and "give me five papers on this" are safe
+ "Summarise this paper I uploaded" is safe; "give me five papers on this" is dangerous
- Both are dangerous
- It depends on the model's knowledge cutoff
= The first is transformation of material in front of the model. The second is recall of facts, which is exactly where invention clusters. Use databases for finding and AI for understanding what you found.

Q. Where does AI help most with a presentation?
- Generating the slides
- Designing the layout
+ Deciding the argument and anticipating objections, before any slides exist
- Writing the speaker notes
= Most presentations fail because the argument was never decided. Twenty minutes on structure and likely objections beats two hours on slides, and auto-generated decks look like presentations without doing what a presentation is for.

Q. What is the safety rule for spreadsheets?
- Never upload a spreadsheet to an AI tool
+ Ask for formulas, not figures -- let the spreadsheet do the arithmetic
- Only use it for Excel, not Google Sheets
- Always ask it to double-check its own arithmetic
= A language model produces plausible-looking numbers rather than calculated ones. Asking for the formula and letting the spreadsheet compute gets the benefit without the risk. Reading numbers off a screenshot has the same problem.

Q. What is the productive division of labour for document writing?
- AI writes the document, you edit it
+ You supply the substance, AI handles the shape
- AI writes the outline, you write the prose
- You write the first draft, AI rewrites it
= You know the constraints, the politics and the history; the model cannot guess them. Writing your thinking down badly in bullets and asking for it to be turned into prose is transformation, which is reliable. "Write me a report" is generation, which is generic.

Q. When asking for help with your own writing, what should you request?
- A rewrite in a more professional tone
+ Critique: what is unclear, what is unsupported, what a reader would ask
- A shorter version
- Three alternative versions
= Critique keeps your voice and improves your thinking. Rewriting replaces both, and heavily AI-edited writing converges on a bland middle register. Most people ask for the rewrite.

Q. What should you add to any email prompt involving specifics?
- "Be professional"
+ "Use only what I have given you"
- "Keep it under 100 words"
- "Write in my voice"
= Without it you get invented reasons, dates, amounts or commitments. This is the same instruction as the structured-output rule from module 4, applied to prose.

Q. What do meeting summaries reliably fail to capture?
- Who attended
- The action items
+ Reluctance, silence, and who actually had the authority to agree
- The topic of the meeting
= A summary records the words. "Fine, we will do it that way" reads exactly like agreement. Nobody objecting is not everybody agreeing. For a meeting that mattered, the summary is an artefact, not a substitute for having been there.

Q. What is the highest-value brainstorming use?
- Asking for thirty ideas instead of five
- Running several constrained rounds
+ Asking for the strongest objections to your plan, ordered by how likely they are to kill it
- Combining ideas from different lists
= People are bad at attacking their own ideas and a tool has no ego about it. Volume and constraints widen the search; adversarial use is what stops you pursuing something that was never going to work.

Q. What is the ten-second habit that matters most with AI search?
- Asking the same question twice
+ Clicking at least one source to see what the answer was built from
- Checking the model's knowledge cutoff
- Rephrasing the question more precisely
= You have outsourced source evaluation. An answer built from official documentation looks identical to one built from a content farm and a forum post. Clicking through is the only way to tell, and the weak sources cluster on commercial and contested questions.
:::

## How to read your score

Seven or more and you are ready for module 7. This is an applied module, so if you missed questions the fix is usually to go and do the demonstrations rather than reread the lessons.

lessons.title: Hands-on lab: automating one real weekly task
lessons.description: Automate one weekly task and measure whether it actually helped.
lessons.content:
Forty-five minutes. You will automate one real task you do every week, and measure whether it actually helped.

The point is not to try ten things. It is to take one thing you genuinely repeat and make it reliably faster.

## Step 1: Pick the task

Go through your last two weeks. Find something you did at least three times that involved writing, summarising, extracting, explaining or formatting.

Strong candidates from this module: a weekly status update; replying to a recurring type of message; turning notes into a structured format; summarising a thread or meeting for someone else; generating practice questions from study material; a spreadsheet task you do by hand.

Write down:

- The task, in one sentence
- How often you do it
- How long it currently takes, honestly
- What "done properly" looks like

That last one becomes your criteria, so be specific.

## Step 2: Time the manual version

Do the task once, by hand, the way you always do. Time it.

Do not skip this. Without a baseline you cannot tell whether you saved time or just enjoyed the novelty, and people consistently misremember how long things took.

## Step 3: Build the prompt

Use module 4 properly: context, task, constraints, format, and the uncertainty instruction.

Mark the variable parts. This is a template, not a one-off.

For anything involving facts, dates, owners or amounts, include **"use only what I have given you"**.

## Step 4: Run it three times

Three real inputs. Fresh conversation each time.

For each run, record:

- The output
- **The total time, including your editing** -- this is the number that matters
- How many of your criteria it met
- What you had to fix

Total time including editing is the honest measure. An output produced in four seconds that takes eleven minutes to fix has not saved you anything.

## Step 5: Improve it once

Look at what you had to fix on all three runs. Find the most common problem.

Change **one thing** in the prompt to address it. Run the three inputs again. Re-record times and scores.

:::hint Nothing needed fixing
Then either the task was easier than you thought, or your criteria are too loose. Tighten them: add a length limit, a required element, or "no claim that is not in the source". Most people who find nothing to fix have not yet checked the output against the source carefully enough.
:::

## Step 6: Decide honestly

Answer these in writing:

1. Manual time versus AI-assisted time, including editing. What actually changed?
2. Was the quality better, worse, or the same?
3. Will you keep doing it this way? Not "could you" -- will you?
4. What would have to change for this to be clearly worth it?

Question 3 is the real test. Most people find roughly a third of tasks they try are worth automating, a third are break-even, and a third are slower. **Reporting a break-even or slower result is a good outcome for this lab**, as long as you have the numbers.

## Step 7: Write it up

1. The task, its frequency, and your criteria
2. Baseline manual time
3. Your prompt, final version
4. The three runs: time, score, what you fixed
5. The one change you made and its effect
6. Your honest decision and what would change it

## What good looks like

**Numbers, not impressions.** "It was faster" is weak. "Manual 22 minutes; AI-assisted 9, 7 and 6 minutes including editing; quality equal on 4 of 5 criteria, worse on tone which I fixed each time" is strong.

**Total time, including editing.** A write-up that reports generation time only has measured the wrong thing.

**An honest verdict.** The most useful submissions are often the ones that conclude it was not worth it, and say precisely why.

lessons.title: Assignment: a personal productivity workflow
lessons.description: A documented personal workflow with evidence, marked against a published rubric.
lessons.content:
## The task

Design and test a **personal AI workflow**: a documented set of ways you will use AI in your own week, with evidence about what worked and honesty about what did not.

This is for you, not for a marker. If it is not something you will still be using in a month, you have built the wrong thing.

## What to submit

One document, **1000 to 1400 words**, in six sections.

### 1. Your week

What you actually do. Study, work, a side project, running something. The recurring tasks -- the things that happen every week whether you feel like it or not.

List at least six. Be specific: not "emails" but "replying to about fifteen enquiries from prospective members".

### 2. The triage

Sort all six or more into four groups, with a reason for each:

- **Automate**: AI does most of it, you check
- **Assist**: AI helps with part, you do the substance
- **Avoid**: AI could do it and should not -- say why
- **Unsuitable**: AI genuinely cannot help

The **avoid** group is the one that shows judgement. Everyone has tasks in it: things where being the person who did it is the point, where the data cannot go into a tool, or where the cost of a confident error is too high. A submission with an empty avoid group has not thought hard enough.

### 3. The workflows

For your top **three** tasks, document the workflow properly:

- The prompt or template, in full, with variable parts marked
- Any standing instructions you set up
- What you check before using the output, specifically
- What you do when it gets it wrong

The "what you check" line is what makes this a workflow rather than a habit.

### 4. The evidence

For each of your three workflows:

- Baseline: how long it took manually, measured not guessed
- At least **three real runs**, with total time including editing
- Your criteria, and how many each run met
- One full worked example: input, prompt, output, your edits

Minimum nine runs across three workflows. Reuse and extend the lab.

### 5. What did not work

At least two things you tried that were not worth it, with the numbers.

This section is marked, and generously. The failures are more useful than the successes, both to you and to a reader deciding whether to bother.

### 6. Your rules

Three to five rules you will actually follow. Each with a reason.

Good rules tend to cover: what you never paste into a tool; what you always verify before sending; when you start fresh rather than continuing; what you disclose and to whom; what you have decided not to use AI for at all.

## Rubric

Marked out of 100.

**Your week, 10 marks.** Full marks for at least six specific, genuinely recurring tasks. Marks lost for vague categories and for tasks you do not actually do weekly.

**The triage, 20 marks.** Full marks where all four groups are used and every placement has a reason. Marks lost heavily for an empty **avoid** group, which is the clearest sign the judgement part was skipped.

**The workflows, 20 marks.** Full marks for three documented workflows with prompts in full, marked variables, a specific checking step and a stated recovery. Marks lost for a prompt with no uncertainty instruction, and for "check the output" as a checking step.

**The evidence, 30 marks.** Full marks for measured baselines, at least nine runs, total time including editing, criteria scores, and one full worked example. This is the heaviest section. Timings that are obviously estimated rather than measured lose marks throughout.

**What did not work, 15 marks.** Full marks for at least two honest failures with numbers and a reason. A submission where everything worked is not believable and scores poorly here.

**Your rules, 5 marks.** Full marks for specific rules with reasons, including at least one thing you will not use AI for.

## What will cost you marks

**Estimated timings presented as measurements.** The difference is obvious to a reader: real timings are uneven and oddly specific, estimates are round numbers.

**Generation time instead of total time.** If your editing is not in the number, the number is wrong.

**An everything-worked submission.** Nobody's first attempt at six workflows all succeeds. This reads as untested.

**Workflows you will not actually use.** Be honest in section 6 if a workflow was interesting and you will not keep it. That is a finding.

**No avoid group.** Repeated because it is the most common way to lose twenty marks on this assignment.

:::hint I cannot find six recurring tasks
Look at your calendar and your sent messages rather than trying to remember. Most people underestimate how much of their week is repeated. Things that qualify: any weekly report or update; any message you send in roughly the same shape more than twice a month; any reading you summarise for someone else; any data you copy from one format to another; any revision or practice routine; any admin that happens on a fixed day. If you genuinely have fewer than six, use a group you belong to and document their week instead of yours.
:::
